scientificName: Macropodidae (eight species recorded near Karma Waters) and Potoroidae (two bettongs)

identification.basis: The dictionary gives English descriptions, not species, and was compiled on the coast. Kadar 'plains wallaby' is most likely the agile wallaby (Notamacropus agilis), the common wallaby of open lowland country and by far the most recorded macropod around Karma Waters; Roth's Cape Bedford 'ga-dar' is the same word. Bimbarrbay 'scrub wallaby' is most likely the red-legged pademelon (Thylogale stigmatica). Julmbanu and mayarriji, the darker and lighter grey kangaroos, are probably the eastern grey (Macropus giganteus), though the whiptail wallaby and the wallaroo may be caught up in them. Nyarrkali 'black kangaroo' may be the dark male common wallaroo (Osphranter robustus) or the swamp wallaby (Wallabia bicolor), also called the black wallaby. Darrba and jumar are not matched to species. Jayju 'kangaroo rat' is a bettong (rufous or northern). Murral/jarrabina is confirmed as a tree-kangaroo, on Eastern Kuku Yalanji country Bennett's (Dendrolagus bennettianus). The Atlas adds the antilopine kangaroo and two rock-wallabies around Karma Waters, for which the dictionary has no words.

summary: Kuku Yalanji has a whole family of words for the hopping animals. **[kadar](word:kadar)** is the 'plains wallaby', **[bimbarrbay](word:bimbarrbay)** the 'scrub wallaby', **[darrba](word:darrba)** the 'grass wallaby' and **[jumar](word:jumar)** the 'little wallaby'. **[julmbanu](word:julmbanu)** and **[mayarriji](word:mayarriji)** are the darker and lighter grey kangaroos, **[nyarrkali](word:nyarrkali)** the 'black kangaroo', **[jayju](word:jayju)** the 'kangaroo rat', and up in the rainforest trees of the coast live **[murral](word:murral)** (Nyungkul **[jarrabina](word:jarrabina)**), the tree-kangaroos [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's 1901 bulletin records every way north Queensland people took them: stalked from downwind in the midday heat, moved onto a hidden spearman with a scent-charged spare spear, driven by beaters into [nets](entry:nets) and cage traps, surrounded by a circle of hunters, pushed by [lines of fire](entry:hunting-with-fire) up to a mile long, run down with [dogs](entry:dingo-and-dogs) in wet weather, and driven off high ground into floodwater [ref:roth1901]. This page gathers the words, the animals, their habits, the recorded hunting methods, the uses of meat, [sinew](entry:sinew), bone and skin, and what the law allows today. The hunting detail is labelled by district, because Roth wrote almost nothing about the Bloomfield itself. Each place below has its own animals and its own record.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary separates the hopping animals by size, colour and the country they live in [ref:hershberger1982]:

- **[kadar](word:kadar)** 'plains wallaby'
- **[bimbarrbay](word:bimbarrbay)** 'scrub wallaby'
- **[darrba](word:darrba)** 'grass wallaby'
- **[jumar](word:jumar)** 'little wallaby'
- **[julmbanu](word:julmbanu)** 'grey kangaroo, a darker variety than mayarriji'
- **[mayarriji](word:mayarriji)** 'sub-species of grey kangaroo, lighter in colour than the "julmbanu"'
- **[nyarrkali](word:nyarrkali)** 'black kangaroo'
- **[jayju](word:jayju)** 'kangaroo rat'
- **[murral](word:murral)** 'tree kangaroo (yalanji) (nyungkul - jarrabina)'; **[jarrabina](word:jarrabina)** 'tree-climbing kangaroo'

All of them are **[minya](word:minya)**, the dictionary's 'meat, eggs (protein food); generic term for animal' [ref:hershberger1982]. The parts have their own words: **[biji](word:biji)** 'tail', **[banda](word:banda)** 'point of tail, tip of tail', **[wurmbu](word:wurmbu)** 'tip of tail or top of tree', **[biyal](word:biyal)** 'gristle, sinew, string, blood vessel (especially wallaby tail sinew)', **[bajibay](word:bajibay)** 'bone', **[yulban](word:yulban)** 'any soft covering such as skin or vegetable or fruit peeling', **[jiba](word:jiba)** 'liver; insides, guts', **[julbi](word:julbi)** 'guts, abdominal contents, lining of abdomen' (Nyungkul **[juwul](word:juwul)**), **[kiru](word:kiru)** 'brains; grease, marrow, drippings from animal fat' and **[wuynkurr](word:wuynkurr)** 'juice of meat' [ref:hershberger1982].

**The hunter's sentence.** The dictionary's example for *[karangaji](word:karangaji)* 'stalk' is a wallaby hunt: *Nyulu dingkar karangajin kadaranda*, 'The man stalked the wallaby' [ref:hershberger1982]. The other verbs of the hunt are *[balbi](word:balbi)* 'hunt for, search for', *[kangal](word:kangal)* 'chase', *[karangal](word:karangal)* 'sneak around to see, reconnoiter', *[mungkil](word:mungkil)* 'spear to kill' and *[mumal](word:mumal)* 'to throw a spear with a woomera'. A good hunter is *[mala-minya](word:mala-minya)* or *[jurru-walay](word:jurru-walay)* 'expert, good shooter or hunter'; *[walay](word:walay)* is 'being good at working or getting food, as a good hunter', and *[majarr](word:majarr)* 'lazy, no good for hunting or working, used to refer to both dogs and people' [ref:hershberger1982].

**The same word up the coast.** Roth's 1901 vocabulary for the Koko-Yimidir (Guugu Yimithirr) language of Cape Bedford gives *ga-dar* as a 'species of kangaroo' [ref:roth1901-b2], plainly the same word as Kuku Yalanji *[kadar](word:kadar)*. On the lower Tully, Roth recorded that the hand sign for 'pouch' also meant 'a wallaby' [ref:roth1902].

**Hand signs for the animals.** In 1908 Roth published the gesture language of several north Queensland districts, used when people needed to be silent, and it has a set of signs for the kangaroo family. In the general sign for kangaroo or wallaby 'the hands (the animal's paws) are held at some distance in front, and motioned forwards and upwards (the hop); in the latter, the same idea, but the hands are held closer to the chest'. At Cape Bedford one kangaroo sign was an extended thumb, which 'some say ... represents the long ear, but the majority that it indicates the long foot'. At Princess Charlotte Bay a male kangaroo was shown by 'the leg kicking out', a female by 'rotation at wrist with the open hand ... the movement of the animal's paws', the brown kangaroo male by 'a vertical flexion of the wrist, indicative of the way the animal travels', and the brown female by 'the pricking up of the animal's ears'. There were separate signs for the scrub-wallaby, the small rock-wallaby, the 'white wallaby' and the paddymelon [ref:roth1908]. Roth did not record the Bloomfield or Palmer signs; whether Yalanji hunters used signs like these is for the contribution box.

sections.heading: The animals: which is which
sections.body:
The kangaroos, wallaroos and wallabies are one family, the Macropodidae, the 'large-foot' animals. 'As with the terms "wallaroo" and "wallaby", "kangaroo" refers to a paraphyletic grouping of species. All three terms refer to members of the same taxonomic family, Macropodidae, and are distinguished according to size. The largest species in the family are called "kangaroos" and the smallest are generally called "wallabies". The term "wallaroos" refers to species of an intermediate size' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The dictionary's split between 'wallaby' and 'kangaroo' is the same kind of split, and like the English one it cuts across the biologists' species [ref:hershberger1982].

**What they all share.** 'Kangaroos have large, powerful hind legs, large feet adapted for leaping, a long muscular tail for balance, and a small head. Like most marsupials, female kangaroos have a pouch called a marsupium in which joeys complete postnatal development' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The foot is the family's signature: 'the fourth toe is very large and strong, the fifth toe moderately so; the second and third are fused; and the first toe is usually missing. Their short front legs have five separate digits' [ref:wiki-macropodidae]. The teeth are a grazer's: 'its incisors are able to crop grass close to the ground and its molars chop and grind the grass. Since the two sides of the lower jaw are not joined or fused together, the lower incisors are farther apart, giving the kangaroo a wider bite' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. Those loose lower incisors are the ones Roth's Pennefather hunters saved for spokeshaves (see *What the animal gave*) [ref:roth1901].

## The animals, one by one

**Agile wallaby** (*Notamacropus agilis*), the most likely *[kadar](word:kadar)* 'plains wallaby'. 'The agile wallaby is a large wallaby with a sandy brown coat, with a white stripe on each side of the face and white stripes on each thigh. It has large ears with black edges. The body and tail length is up to 1.8 m. Males weigh up to 27 kg, while females are around 15 kg. The tip of the tail is black' [ref:nesp-agile]. 'It is the most common wallaby in north Australia' [ref:wiki-agile]. 'They can be active during the day or night. Agile wallabies often rest quietly in the shade during the day, and graze on grasses, legumes, fallen fruits and other herbs in the late afternoon. They are often seen in small groups' [ref:nesp-agile].

**Common wallaroo** (*Osphranter robustus*). It is 'also known as the euro, hill wallaroo, or simply wallaroo'. Two forms meet somewhere in Queensland: 'the eastern wallaroo (*O. r. robustus*), which is dark grey in colour, occupies the eastern slopes of the Great Dividing Range, and the euro (*O. r. erubescens*), which is mostly brownish in colour, occupies the land westward'. 'The eastern wallaroo is mostly nocturnal and solitary, and is one of the more common macropods. It can make a loud hissing noise. All four subspecies are sexually dimorphic' [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. The dark grey male wallaroo is one candidate for *[nyarrkali](word:nyarrkali)* 'black kangaroo' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Eastern grey kangaroo** (*Macropus giganteus*), the big grey of the open country and the likeliest *[julmbanu](word:julmbanu)* and *[mayarriji](word:mayarriji)* [ref:hershberger1982]. 'The eastern grey kangaroo is the second largest and heaviest living marsupial and native land mammal in Australia. An adult male will commonly weigh around 50 to 66 kg whereas females commonly weigh around 17 to 40 kg. They have a powerful tail that is over 1 m long in adult males' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]. 'Like all kangaroos, it is mainly nocturnal and crepuscular, and is mostly seen early in the morning, or as the light starts to fade in the evening. In the middle of the day, kangaroos rest in the cover of the woodlands' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey].

**Whiptail wallaby** (*Notamacropus parryi*). 'Also known as the pretty-faced wallaby ... It is locally common from Cooktown in Queensland to near Grafton in New South Wales'. 'It is distinguished by its paler colouring and white stripe under its face. Their faces have a chocolate-brown fur covering their muzzle. They are black and white on its chest and the rest is grey to brown fur. Males weigh from 14 to 26 kg and stand at a height from 70 to 93 cm. Females weigh from 7 to 15 kg' [ref:wiki-whiptail]. Its pale colour and hill country make it a candidate for the lighter grey *[mayarriji](word:mayarriji)* or for *[darrba](word:darrba)* 'grass wallaby'; the dictionary does not say.

**Antilopine kangaroo** (*Osphranter antilopinus*). It is 'found in northern Australia: in Cape York Peninsula in Queensland, the Top End of the Northern Territory, and the Kimberley region of Western Australia. It is a locally common, gregarious grazer'. 'The fur is short, pale at the ventral side and grading to a reddish tan colour over the upper parts'. Males stand about 1.1 m at the crown and 'may be over twice' the female's 20 kg, 'at 49 kilograms' [ref:wiki-antilopine]. This is the kangaroo of the lowland grass plains, 'only found at altitudes less than 500 metres' [ref:wiki-antilopine].

**Mareeba rock-wallaby** (*Petrogale mareeba*). 'The Mareeba rock-wallaby is a rare species, found in the highlands west of Cairns from around Mount Garnet to the Mitchell River and Mount Carbine, and inland to Mungana, but only on the tops of a couple of mountain ranges' [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby]. It is 'near-threatened' on the world list but 'least concern' under Queensland's *Nature Conservation Act 1992* [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby].

**Godman's rock-wallaby** (*Petrogale godmani*), the rock-wallaby of the Cooktown side. 'This rock-wallaby is found in low open forest, open scrub, or montane regions, often near the coast. It shelters in rocky terrain adjacent to feeding areas. Godman's rock-wallaby is a nocturnal gregarious territorial folivore' [ref:wiki-godman]. The dictionary, compiled on the coast, has no rock-wallaby word; the Western Yalanji name for the little grey kangaroo of the rock piles is for the contribution box [ref:hershberger1982].

**Red-legged pademelon** (*Thylogale stigmatica*), the most likely *[bimbarrbay](word:bimbarrbay)* 'scrub wallaby' [ref:hershberger1982]. It 'is found mostly in rainforests, where it is rarely seen'. 'Pademelons have a short and thick tail, and their height can range from 35–58 cm when not standing upright ... their weight varies from 2.5 to 7 kg'. 'Red-legged pademelons are unique in that they are the only ground-dwelling wallaby that resides in the Wet Tropics rainforests' [ref:wiki-pademelon].

**The two bettongs**, the 'rat-kangaroos', are the dictionary's *[jayju](word:jayju)* 'kangaroo rat' country [ref:hershberger1982]. The rufous bettong (*Aepyprymnus rufescens*) is 'a small, jumping, rat-like marsupial native to eastern Australia ... about the size of a rabbit. The rufous rat-kangaroo is active at night when it digs for plant roots and fungi'; it 'is found in coastal and subcoastal regions from Newcastle in New South Wales to Cooktown in Queensland' [ref:wiki-rufous-bettong]. The northern bettong (*Bettongia tropica*) 'is a small, endangered, rabbit-sized mammal native to forests in northeast Australia ... it moves by hopping and shelters in a concealed nest by day, feeding at night on roots and fungi'. 'It is estimated that there are only 1000 left in the wild' [ref:wiki-northern-bettong].

**On the coast.** Bennett's tree-kangaroo, the *[murral](word:murral)* of Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, 'is found in both mountain and lowland tropical rain forests south of Cooktown, Queensland to just north of the Daintree River; an area of only about 70 by 50 km' [ref:wiki-bennett]. The swamp wallaby (*Wallabia bicolor*), 'also commonly known as the black wallaby', 'is found from the northernmost areas of Cape York Peninsula in Queensland, down the entire east coast' [ref:wiki-swamp-wallaby]; on the Bloomfield it is the other candidate for *[nyarrkali](word:nyarrkali)* 'black kangaroo', and the question is open.

## Which dictionary word is which animal?

The dictionary gives English descriptions, not species, and it was compiled with coastal speakers [ref:hershberger1982]. Putting the animals beside the word list:

- *[kadar](word:kadar)* 'plains wallaby': **agile wallaby**, probable. It is the common wallaby of open lowland country [ref:wiki-agile], and Cape Bedford *ga-dar* is the same word [ref:roth1901-b2].
- *[bimbarrbay](word:bimbarrbay)* 'scrub wallaby': **red-legged pademelon**, probable, the one ground wallaby of the rainforest [ref:wiki-pademelon].
- *[darrba](word:darrba)* 'grass wallaby': **whiptail wallaby**, or a second name for the agile; uncertain.
- *[jumar](word:jumar)* 'little wallaby': a young animal, a pademelon or a bettong; uncertain.
- *[julmbanu](word:julmbanu)* and *[mayarriji](word:mayarriji)*, the darker and lighter grey kangaroos: **eastern grey kangaroo**, probable, perhaps with the wallaroo or the whiptail caught up in the pair.
- *[nyarrkali](word:nyarrkali)* 'black kangaroo': the **dark male wallaroo** or the **swamp wallaby**; uncertain.
- *[jayju](word:jayju)* 'kangaroo rat': the **rufous or northern bettong**, probable.
- *[murral](word:murral)* and *[jarrabina](word:jarrabina)* 'tree kangaroo': **Bennett's tree-kangaroo**, confirmed.

Nothing in this list should be read as the last word. The people who hunt these animals know which is which, and that knowledge belongs in the contribution box, not in a guess.

sections.heading: Telling them apart
sections.body:
Out on the flats in the half-light, size and colour are what you have, and the family is good at looking alike. These are the field marks from the published descriptions.

**Agile wallaby or whiptail wallaby?** Both are mid-sized, both graze open grass, both have a white face stripe. The agile is 'sandy brown' with 'white stripes on each thigh', 'large ears with black edges' and a black tail tip [ref:nesp-agile]. The whiptail is paler, with a 'chocolate-brown fur covering their muzzle' and a 'black and white' chest, and it carries the long thin tail that gives it its name [ref:wiki-whiptail]. The whiptail is 'primarily a diurnal species ... active in the morning and late in the afternoon' and 'sometimes coming together in mobs of up to 50', while the agile 'is a solitary animal, but it sometimes forms into groups when feeding on open pastures' and 'feeds mainly at night' [ref:wiki-whiptail] [ref:wiki-agile]. A big daytime mob of pale wallabies on a hillside is the whiptail; a scatter of sandy ones along the river flat at dusk is the agile.

**Eastern grey or wallaroo?** The eastern grey is the bigger, with the male 'around 50 to 66 kg' and a tail 'over 1 m long' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]; its muzzle is 'fully covered with fine hair', which is one of the points that separate the greys from 'reds and wallaroos' with their bare noses [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]. The wallaroo is stockier and darker, the eastern form 'dark grey', the euro 'mostly brownish' [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. Habit separates them as well as colour: the grey is 'gregarious and form[s] open-membership groups' and grazes the open country at dawn and dusk [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]; the wallaroo is 'mostly nocturnal and solitary' and hisses loudly when alarmed [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. The 'hill wallaroo' is well named [ref:wiki-wallaroo]: look for it on the stony ridges, and for the grey on the grass between them.

**Wallaroo or antilopine?** On the lowland plains the reddish-tan male antilopine, with 'longer and more slender limbs' and a group of up to 30 around it, is the one that does not look like a wallaroo at all [ref:wiki-antilopine]. The female antilopine is 'lighter and with greyish fur' and can pass for a grey at a distance [ref:wiki-antilopine].

**Rock-wallaby or anything else?** A small grey-brown wallaby on a boulder slope or granite outcrop, that goes up the rocks rather than across the flat, is a rock-wallaby. On the Mitchell side that is the Mareeba rock-wallaby, 'only on the tops of a couple of mountain ranges' [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby]; on the Cooktown side Godman's, 'often near the coast', nocturnal and 'in rocky terrain adjacent to feeding areas' [ref:wiki-godman].

**Scrub wallaby or little wallaby?** The pademelon is small, 2.5 to 7 kg, with 'a short and thick tail' [ref:wiki-pademelon], and it keeps to the rainforest edge, grazing 'on open grassland near the rainforest edges but quickly retreat[ing] into the forest if disturbed' [ref:wiki-pademelon]. The swamp wallaby is larger, about 13 to 17 kg, dark 'brown to black' on the back with a cheek stripe and often a white tail tip, and it browses shrubs rather than grazing [ref:wiki-swamp-wallaby].

**Kangaroo rat or rat?** The bettongs hop. The rufous bettong is rabbit-sized, 'generally grey with a hint of reddish brown', with 'ruffled and bristly hair' and 'an indistinct stripe ... at the hip line'; it is 'strictly nocturnal' and nests under 'a dense under-story of vegetation' [ref:wiki-rufous-bettong]. The northern bettong is the same size, nests by day 'beneath a tree, within a clump of grass or in other litter', and digs for underground fungi [ref:wiki-northern-bettong]. Neither should be confused with the [bandicoots and rats](entry:quolls-bandicoots-and-rats), which run on four legs.

**Joey or adult?** A young animal out of the pouch is a small copy of its mother and stays with her: whiptail joeys 'follow their mothers continuously and do not hide in vegetation' [ref:wiki-whiptail], and in the eastern grey 'the female ... is usually permanently pregnant except on the day she gives birth' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey], so a mob always carries young. The dictionary's *[jumar](word:jumar)* 'little wallaby' may be a size word as much as a species word [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs: tracks, scats, pads and scent
sections.body:
The old hunting was mostly reading the ground before the animal was ever seen. See the [tracks and signs](entry:tracks-and-signs) page for the general method; this is the kangaroo family's part of it.

**Tracks.** 'All wallabies in Australia have similar tracks. Wallabies have 5 clawed toes on the front foot, and these toes point forward. They have a long hind foot. The long fourth toe, with its large strong claw, and the shorter fifth toe, also with a strong claw, are the only ones that touch the ground when the wallaby moves. The second and third toes are joined up to their top joints, with claws used for grooming' [ref:nesp-agile]. A hopping animal leaves the two long hind prints side by side; a feeding animal walking slowly leaves the tail and the small front paws as well, because 'kangaroos have a unique three-stage walk where they plant their front legs and tail first, then push off their tail, followed lastly by the back legs' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. 'The agile wallaby hops with its body held upright, its head held high and with forearms extended' [ref:nesp-agile]. The bigger the animal, the longer the hind print and the wider the gap between hops. The dictionary's **[baral](word:baral)** is 'road, path, track, trail' and **[jinabu dungay](word:jinabu dungay)** 'to go by foot' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Pads to water.** Kangaroos and wallabies wear 'beaten tracks to water', and Roth's North-West hunters rigged their nets along them [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1897]. At Atherton the nets were 'fixed across the tracks leading from the mountains, etc., to the water-holes' [ref:roth1901].

**Scats.** Agile wallaby scats 'are usually seen in groups of four to eight around their feeding areas and sleeping places. Groups of scats from the same animal may vary in shape (oval, round, or slightly square shaped), and are 10–12 mm in width and filled with grass or plants' [ref:nesp-agile]. The bigger kangaroos leave bigger, squarer pellets; fresh ones are dark and moist, old ones pale and dry.

**Cropped grass and camps.** The family's incisors 'crop grass close to the ground' [ref:wiki-kangaroo], so a grazed flat looks mown. Eastern greys 'rest in the cover of the woodlands' in the middle of the day [ref:wiki-eastern-grey] and agile wallabies 'rest quietly in the shade' [ref:nesp-agile]: a worn hollow of bare earth under a shady tree, with scats around it, is a day camp.

**Scent.** 'These animals having a very sensitive appreciation of [the hunter's] scent' was Roth's note from the Palmer, Musgrave and Princess Charlotte Bay, and the whole stalking method there was built around it [ref:roth1901]. Anderson's Bloomfield hunters 'stalked from down wind at times and places where they were known to graze, rest or come for water' [ref:anderson1996]. The dictionary's words are **[jila](word:jila)** 'beeswax; smell; sweat', **[nyumal](word:nyumal)** 'to smell or taste' and **[muyar](word:muyar)** 'wind' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Ears, and what they hear.** Roth's drives moved the animals with noise: at Atherton 'the kangaroo, driven headlong by the shouts of the hunters', and the wallabies by women and children 'shouting and hooting' [ref:roth1901]. The dictionary has the hunter's quiet words: **[kiray](word:kiray)** 'slow, quiet', **[janka](word:janka)** 'quiet', **[muwul](word:muwul)** 'secretly, quietly', **[durrubu dungay](word:durrubu dungay)** 'walk on tiptoe', and for the opposite **[nyurra-baka](word:nyurra-baka)** 'people making too much noise' and **[yanja](word:yanja)** 'rustling noise, as the wind blowing through trees or grass' [ref:hershberger1982]. The hand signs Roth recorded exist because the hunters did not talk [ref:roth1908].

**The alarm.** A wallaroo 'can make a loud hissing noise' [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. Pademelons 'are often found in small groups, foraging 30–50 m apart so that they can warn each other of oncoming predators' [ref:wiki-pademelon]. The whiptail mob has lookouts: 'the members of the mob take turns resting and guarding' [ref:wiki-whiptail]. When one animal stands bolt upright with its ears forward, the mob has seen you. The dictionary's **[jiba-warri](word:jiba-warri)** is 'become startled', **[jiba-yararri](word:jiba-yararri)** 'frightened', **[yinyil-kangal](word:yinyil-kangal)** 'to frighten' and **[minday](word:minday)** 'tame, quiet, brave, not afraid of or shy of, confident' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Fire scars and green pick.** The dictionary's **[duli](word:duli)** is 'burnt patch of grass' and **[ngalku](word:ngalku)** 'bush fire' [ref:hershberger1982]. Regular burning 'encouraged those animals which were favoured by more open country', and 'had the long-term effect of turning dry forest into savanna, increasing the populations of grass-eating animals such as kangaroos' [ref:wiki-fire-stick]. A patch burnt weeks ago, greening up, draws grazers; a patch burnt yesterday repels them. Cook saw that on the Endeavour River: kangaroos 'so much afraid of fire that our dogs could scarcely force it over places which had been newly burnt, though the fire was extinguished' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.body:
**Open woodland and grass.** This is the family's country. 'Agile wallabies live in open forest, tropical woodlands and grasslands and on coastal sand dunes, especially near water. They are common in northern Australia and parts of the east coast of Queensland' [ref:nesp-agile]; a habitat model built from desert surveys found that 'agile wallabies prefer areas of higher annual rainfall (over 500 mm) that are close to water (<1 km)' [ref:nesp-agile]. The eastern grey 'is predominantly a grazer, and eats a wide variety of grasses' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The whiptail 'lives in grasslands and woodlands particularly on hills or slopes ... In grasslands, the whiptail wallaby primarily eats kangaroo grass. It also eats monocots in nearby creeks' [ref:wiki-whiptail]. The antilopine likes 'perennial grasses providing forage, in vegetation occurring over lower hills and plains ... in association with monsoonal eucalypts, as open or regenerating woodlands' [ref:wiki-antilopine].

**The ridges and the rocks.** The wallaroo is the 'hill wallaroo' [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. The Mareeba rock-wallaby lives 'only on the tops of a couple of mountain ranges' between Mount Garnet, the Mitchell River, Mount Carbine and Mungana [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby]; Godman's 'shelters in rocky terrain adjacent to feeding areas' [ref:wiki-godman].

**The river.** Kangaroos are tied to water in the dry, and the river is where the pads lead [ref:roth1901]. But it is no fence: 'kangaroos and wallabies are adept swimmers, and often flee into waterways if presented with the option. If pursued into the water, a large kangaroo may use its forepaws to hold the predator underwater so as to drown it' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. Roth's lower Tully people turned that around in flood time, driving wallabies 'from off the higher levels into the water, and there soon dispose[d] of them with sticks and spears' [ref:roth1901].

**Rainforest and its edges.** The pademelon keeps to 'rainforest areas' and grazes their edges [ref:wiki-pademelon]. The northern bettong 'is restricted to some areas of mixed open *Eucalyptus* woodlands and *Allocasuarina* forests bordering rainforests in far northeastern Queensland' [ref:wiki-northern-bettong]. The dictionary's country words are **[madja](word:madja)** 'scrub, jungle, rain forest', **[kuri](word:kuri)** 'small patch of scrub', **[jamar](word:jamar)** 'newly cleared scrub', **[ngalkal](word:ngalkal)** 'outside ... the scrub', **[jikan](word:jikan)** 'grass' and **[wabarr](word:wabarr)** 'shade' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How they live
sections.body:
**Grazing and the gut.** 'Modern macropods are generally herbivorous. Some are browsers, but most are grazers and are equipped with appropriately specialised teeth for cropping and grinding up fibrous plants, in particular grasses and sedges' [ref:wiki-macropodidae]. 'Like the eutherian ruminants of the Northern Hemisphere (sheep, cattle, and so on), macropods have specialised digestive systems that use a high concentration of bacteria, protozoans, and fungi in the first chamber of a complex stomach to digest plant material' [ref:wiki-macropodidae], and 'despite having herbivorous diets similar to ruminants such as cattle, which release large quantities of digestive methane ... kangaroos release virtually none' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. 'The ability of larger macropods to survive on poor-quality, low-energy feed, and to travel long distances at high speed without great energy expenditure (to reach fresh food supplies or waterholes, and to escape predators) has been crucial to their evolutionary success' [ref:wiki-macropodidae]. The swamp wallaby is the browser of the family, eating 'shrubs and bushes, rather than grazing on grasses' and tolerating 'a variety of plants poisonous to many other animals' [ref:wiki-swamp-wallaby]. The bettongs eat underground: ectomycorrhizal fungi are 'the staple diet of the northern bettong. These are dug from beneath the soil at the bases of trees' [ref:wiki-northern-bettong], and the rufous bettong 'digs for plant roots and fungi' [ref:wiki-rufous-bettong].

**The hop, and why the sinew matters.** 'Kangaroos are the only large mammals to use hopping on two legs as their primary means of locomotion. The comfortable hopping speed for a red kangaroo is about 20–25 km/h, but speeds of up to 70 km/h can be attained over short distances, while it can sustain a speed of 40 km/h for nearly 2 km' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. 'The highest recorded jump for a red kangaroo is about 10 feet (3.0 m), whereas for the eastern grey kangaroo it is 8 feet (2.4 m)' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The engine is tendon: 'kangaroos and wallabies have large, elastic tendons in their hind legs. They store elastic strain energy in the tendons of their large hind legs, providing most of the energy required for each hop by the spring action of the tendons rather than by any muscular effort', and 'increased speed requires very little extra effort' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The tail is a fifth leg: in the slow walk 'the propulsive force of the tail is equal to that of both the front and hind legs combined' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The same tendons are the hunter's *[biyal](word:biyal)*, 'especially wallaby tail sinew' [ref:hershberger1982], which is why the tail tendons came out first at the kill (see *What the animal gave*) [ref:roth1901].

**Day and night.** The grazers are animals of the edges of the day. The eastern grey 'is mainly nocturnal and crepuscular, and is mostly seen early in the morning, or as the light starts to fade in the evening. In the middle of the day, kangaroos rest in the cover of the woodlands' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]. The agile 'feeds mainly at night on grasses, legumes, and other herbaceous plants, but may also forage by day, especially in the wet season' [ref:wiki-agile]. The Queensland Government's plain summary is that 'kangaroos are active during the day but mostly feed at dawn and dusk' [ref:qld-kangaroos]. The whiptail is the exception, 'primarily a diurnal species', with its mob gathering 'in the afternoon during feeding' [ref:wiki-whiptail]. The wallaroo and the rock-wallabies are night animals [ref:wiki-wallaroo] [ref:wiki-godman], and the bettongs 'will only emerge after sunset and return to the nest before first light' [ref:wiki-rufous-bettong]. Roth's North-West hunters used the day habit: kangaroos 'may be tracked and sneaked upon during the extreme midday heat, and caught while resting in the shade' [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1897].

**Mobs, sentries and the nose.** 'Groups of kangaroos are called mobs, courts or troupes, which usually have 10 or more kangaroos in them. Living in mobs can provide protection for some of the weaker members of the group' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. Eastern grey groups 'contain an average of three individuals. Smaller groups join to graze in preferred foraging areas, and to rest in large groups around the middle of the day' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]. The antilopine 'forms social groupings ... up to 30 individuals, but these may be separate groups assembling as a response to threats from humans or dingoes' [ref:wiki-antilopine]. The whiptail mob of up to 50 posts guards [ref:wiki-whiptail]. Kangaroos read each other by smell: 'one common behaviour is nose touching and sniffing, which mostly occurs when an individual joins a group ... The kangaroo performing the sniffing gains much information from smell cues' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. An animal that smells people as sharply as that is the animal Roth's hunters stalked from downwind [ref:roth1901].

**Fights.** 'Fighting has been described in all species of kangaroos. Fights between kangaroos can be brief or long and ritualised. In highly competitive situations, such as males fighting for access to oestrous females or at limited drinking spots, the fights are brief' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. 'A winner is decided when a kangaroo breaks off the fight and retreats. Winners are able to push their opponents backwards or down to the ground' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. Male agile wallabies 'play-fight', 'leaping into the air, and sinuously lashing the tail' [ref:wiki-agile]. At a dry-season waterhole the big males are at their most short-tempered, which is one reason to keep clear of them (see *Safety*).

**Joeys.** 'As with all marsupials, the young are born at a very early stage of development, after a gestation of 31–36 days. At this stage, only the forelimbs are somewhat developed, to allow the newborn to climb to the pouch and attach to a teat' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. 'Typically, only a single young is born, weighing less than 1 g at birth ... The young leave the pouch after five to 11 months' [ref:wiki-macropodidae]. The mother 'has the ability to freeze the development of an embryo until the previous joey is able to leave the pouch. This is known as embryonic diapause and will occur in times of drought and in areas with poor food sources' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. In the wallaroo 'the young joeys start to leave the pouch at around six months and by nine months they no longer spend most of their time in the pouch' [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. Whiptail joeys 'stay in their mothers' pouches for the first nine months. When they leave, they will still stay with them for up to 18 months' [ref:wiki-whiptail].

**Predators.** 'With the arrival of humans in Australia at least 50,000 years ago and the introduction of the dingo about 5,000 years ago, kangaroos have had to adapt' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]; today 'along with dingoes, introduced species such as foxes, feral cats, and both domestic and feral dogs, pose a threat to kangaroo populations' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. The pademelon's 'main predators ... are dingoes, tiger quolls, Australian scrub pythons, and occasionally feral domestic dogs. The rate of predation increases following a forest fire, when there is less forest cover' [ref:wiki-pademelon]. The swamp wallaby's are 'dingoes, eagles and wild dogs' [ref:wiki-swamp-wallaby]. Roth recorded the hunting partnership from the other side: [dingo](entry:dingo-and-dogs) pups 'caught young, brought into camp, and tied up by the leg until such time as they become reconciled to their surroundings', and on the Bloomfield a boy put in charge of them [ref:roth1901].

**Fire and the family.** The long story is that Aboriginal burning 'had the long-term effect of turning dry forest into savanna, increasing the populations of grass-eating animals such as kangaroos' [ref:wiki-fire-stick]. The short story is in the record of one fire: after 'a huge fire raged through the Yourka Reserve near Einasleigh ... in December 2019, part of the 2019–2020 bushfires in Australia, it was feared that the rock-wallaby population might not survive. However, it was found that the population was thriving, with several new joeys spotted in their mothers' pouches' [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby].

**Cattle and kangaroos.** 'Unlike many of the smaller macropods, kangaroos have fared well since European settlement. European settlers cut down forests to create vast grasslands for sheep and cattle grazing, added stock watering points in arid areas, and have substantially reduced the number of dingoes' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]. Whether that holds on a lightly stocked Cape York station is not something anyone has measured; the small members of the family have not fared so well, and the northern bettong is down to about a thousand [ref:wiki-northern-bettong].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
**Any time, in the old record.** Roth's rule for the whole of north Queensland was that 'speaking generally: emu, kangaroo, opossum, and fish are hunted at any time; lilies and honey in the dry season; roots and fruits in the wet season' [ref:roth1901]. The fat rule qualified that: an animal *[jirrburr](word:jirrburr)*, 'meat with no fat, an animal in poor condition', 'will not be eaten' [ref:hershberger1982], so the hunting season was really the fat season of each animal.

**The wet: floods, bogs and dogs.** Two of Roth's methods belong to the wet. On the lower Tully 'in flood-time ... [people] drive the wallabies from off the higher levels into the water, and there soon dispose of them with sticks and spears' [ref:roth1901]; in the North-West 'in rainy weather, and over boggy soil, they are run down with dogs' [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1897]. The agile wallaby 'may also forage by day, especially in the wet season', and 'in the dry season, the animal's range grows larger as the quality of the grazing deteriorates' [ref:wiki-agile].

**The hot time before the storms.** On Cape York 'by the late dry, fuels are completely dry and fires can be severe and widespread. Storm burns are lit after the first storm rains, normally between October and January' [ref:pbg-cape-york]. The late dry is when the grazers are tightest on the last water and the shade, and when a grass fire is most dangerous. The [seasons](entry:seasons) page has the Kuku Yalanji year; the dictionary's **[muduwaju](word:muduwaju)** 'dawn, daybreak, early morning', **[wunkuwingku](word:wunkuwingku)** 'morning', **[yilay-yilay](word:yilay-yilay)** 'late afternoon, when the sun is in the west' and **[wujurr](word:wujurr)** 'darkness, night' are the hunter's clock within the day [ref:hershberger1982].

**Breeding through the year.** 'Breeding takes place at any time of the year' in the agile wallaby [ref:wiki-agile]; wallaroo 'females can give birth at any time during the year' [ref:wiki-wallaroo]; in the antilopine 'breeding may occur at any time of the year, although births tend to be timed to precede the beginning of the north's wet season' [ref:wiki-antilopine]; in the eastern grey 'most kangaroo births occur during the summer' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]. A female with a joey at foot is a female with a joey at foot in any month.

sections.heading: What the animal gave
sections.body:
**Meat.** 'Kangaroo meat is very high in protein (23.2%) and very low in fat (2.6%)' [ref:wiki-kangaroo-meat]; 'its low fat content prevents kangaroo meat from being cooked in the same way as other red meats, so it is typically either slow-cooked or quickly stir-fried' [ref:wiki-kangaroo-meat]. That leanness is why the dictionary's fat words carry so much weight. *[Kunukunu](word:kunukunu)* is 'fat in food or fatty meat', *[jilu](word:jilu)* 'an animal that is a little fat', *[wandul](word:wandul)* 'fat'; *[jirrburr](word:jirrburr)* is 'meat with no fat, an animal in poor condition. (This kind of animal will not be eaten)', and *[yulkur](word:yulkur)* 'poor physical condition, lean' [ref:hershberger1982]. See the [cooking meat](entry:cooking-meat) page for the full kitchen; the earth-oven and whole-roast methods are under *The hunt*.

**Sinew.** *[Biyal](word:biyal)* is 'gristle, sinew, string, blood vessel (especially wallaby tail sinew)' [ref:hershberger1982], and it has its own page, [sinew](entry:sinew). On the Pennefather a kangaroo 'on being killed, is usually first of all robbed of its tail-tendons' [ref:roth1901]. At Princess Charlotte Bay the bone barb of the [fish-hook](entry:hooks-and-lines) was fixed to its wooden shank with 'kangaroo-tail tendon, and *Grevillea* gum-cement' [ref:roth1901]; in the Boulia district the hook was bound 'with tendon obtained from kangaroo-tail, emu-leg, or snake-neck', and the woomera peg 'tied on' with tendon through holes 'drilled with a sharpened emu or kangaroo bone' [ref:roth1897]. On the Bloomfield 'the stingray barbs and the multiple-prongs were held in place by wallaby sinew and resins' [ref:anderson1996]. Cape Bedford, which had no wallaby country to speak of, imported it: in return for iron tomahawks, shells and dilly-bags 'they obtain forehead-bands, kangaroo-tail sinew, kangaroo bones (of a certain kind to be specially used for making bone awls), quartz-tipped spears, bark troughs, and a rough kind of fixed grind-stone' [ref:roth1910b14].

**Bone.** The stiletto or awl of Roth's north Queensland, 'from 6 to 8½ inches long', was 'made either of bone (kangaroo, wallaby, emu) or of "iron-wood"' [ref:roth1904]. Kangaroo bone made the barb of the Palmer River hook [ref:roth1901] and the barb of Pennefather [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:roth1909]. 'Knuckle and similar bones from the kangaroo or dingo, and up to about 2½ inches in length', hung as ornaments at the temples in the Boulia district [ref:roth1897].

**Teeth.** The kangaroo's lower incisor was a cutting tool across the northern peninsula. The scraper of the Pennefather and the Batavia was 'a flat leaf-and-stalk shaped piece of "ironwood"' with 'a kangaroo's lower incisor ... fixed with gut, or fibre-twine, and cement: its tip has been previously put into the edge of a flame and broken off abruptly by well-directed and graduated pressure, so as to give a sharp cutting-edge to the enamel'; it was 'employed for sharpening spear-tips, and, in some spears, for cutting the groove into which the barb is fixed' [ref:roth1904]. In the same districts 'half the lower jaw of the kangaroo, with tooth in situ, is employed for similar purposes ... it forms a staple article of barter' [ref:roth1904]. At Princess Charlotte Bay 'the tooth-drill ... is made with an incisor, from any of the larger species of kangaroo, which is stuck into a short handle, and fixed in position with twine and cement' [ref:roth1904]. That is why the Pennefather cook skewered the tongue 'over the incisors (required for spoke-shaves) to prevent them being too much damaged by the heat' [ref:roth1901].

**Hair and skin.** Kangaroo and possum hair was spun into twine for necklaces and belts in the North-West [ref:roth1910b15]. Nearer home, 'the opossum- (or kangaroo) twine waist-belt (KMI. *aln-jo*) of the Middle Palmer and Tully Rivers' was tied in front [ref:roth1910b15]; Roth's KMI is the Koko-Minni of the middle Palmer, Western Yalanji's near neighbours. On the Bloomfield the women's fringed circlet was 'usually manufactured on a core of human-hair overcast with kangaroo- or opossum-hair twine' [ref:roth1910b15]. On the Pennefather 'a strip of kangaroo-skin tied at the ends, forms an ornament ... that is used by women only' [ref:roth1910b15]. Skin water-bags were a North-West thing: 'made from kangaroo, paddymelon, or opossum, the skin is cut all the way round, high up in the neck, the front-paws and tail removed close to their bases, and the whole skin pulled away inside out from the carcass: it is subsequently tanned with bloodwood gum' [ref:roth1897]. There is no record of kangaroo-skin cloaks or bags on the Bloomfield, where the blanket was [paperbark](entry:paperbark) [ref:anderson1996].

**Carrying.** The Bloomfield men's bag, the *ngunyin* of Anderson's account, 'was made from *Ficus* fibre-twine. It was said by Kuku-Yalanji to have been able to stretch big enough to carry a small wallaby' [ref:anderson1996]. Idriess, as Anderson reports him, 'describes wallaby sinew or plaited hair belts which were worn by men and in which they carried their stone axes' [ref:anderson1996].

**Play and pets.** Among the Kalkadun of the North-West the ball game played by jumping to catch a ball 'made of a piece of opossum, wallaby, or kangaroo hide' was called 'the kangaroo-play', and in their 'coursing' game 'a wallaby, dingo, rat, etc., having been previously caught alive' was let go and had to be caught 'with the hands only' [ref:roth1902]. On the lower Tully 'pets may also be made of the ring-tailed opossum and the wallaby, both animals often straying away from "home" for hours at a time' [ref:roth1902]. At Bloomfield, Anderson reports from Idriess, 'cassowaries, wallabies, turtles and birds were kept as the pets of individuals' [ref:anderson1996]. The [games](entry:games-and-string-figures) page has more.

**Dressing for the hunt.** 'During ceremonies and on some hunting trips, prominent Kuku-Yalanji men wore a head ornament consisting of a tuft of cockatoo top-knot feathers stuck into beeswax', and 'body painting was done for some hunting trips' with [red and yellow ochre](entry:red-ochre), charcoal and white clay [ref:anderson1996]. On the Pennefather the paint was camouflage, and it is described under *The hunt* [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: The hunt: the recorded methods, district by district
sections.body:
Roth wrote almost nothing about how the Bloomfield people hunted the wallaby, and nothing at all about the Mitchell. What follows is the published record for the districts of north Queensland, each labelled by place, plus what the animals' own habits say. It is a record, not a manual, and the law section below governs what any of it can mean today.

## 1. Before you go: the four things that decide a hunt

1. **The wind.** Every stalking record agrees. On the Palmer, the Musgrave and the back of Princess Charlotte Bay, 'kangaroos are speared, being tracked from the windward, these animals having a very sensitive appreciation of [the hunter's] scent' [ref:roth1901]; on the Bloomfield they were 'stalked from down wind' [ref:anderson1996]. Roth's 'from the windward' and Anderson's 'from down wind' describe the same position: the hunter keeps the wind in his face, so that his scent blows back behind him and away from the animal. The dictionary's wind is **[muyar](word:muyar)** and the dry-season trade wind **[kumbamu](word:kumbamu)** 'trade wind, fair wind' [ref:hershberger1982]. Smoke from the [campfire](entry:camps-and-firewood) tells you the wind before you leave.
2. **The hour.** The grazers are on the open grass at first light and last light and in the shade through the day [ref:wiki-eastern-grey] [ref:nesp-agile] [ref:qld-kangaroos]. Roth's inland hunters took them in the shade 'during the extreme midday heat' [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1897]. Early morning is also the time the tracks are freshest: the wildlife surveyors' advice is to 'survey during good conditions (in the early morning is best, not too windy or straight after rain)' [ref:nesp-agile].
3. **The water.** In the dry the animals' 'beaten tracks to water' are where the nets went [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1897], and 'times and places where they were known to graze, rest or come for water' are where the Bloomfield stalk began [ref:anderson1996].
4. **The retreat.** An animal that is disturbed goes somewhere, and the old drives all worked by knowing where. The Atherton wallaby 'when ... hard pressed and makes for shelter it runs with the head down' along 'its accustomed tracks' [ref:roth1901]; the Atherton kangaroo nets stood 'across the tracks leading from the mountains, etc., to the water-holes' [ref:roth1901]; the Bloomfield fire wall had 'only a few openings' and the spearmen stood in them [ref:anderson1996]. The grey goes for 'the cover of the woodlands' [ref:wiki-eastern-grey], the pademelon for the forest [ref:wiki-pademelon], the wallaroo for the hill, and any of them for the river if it is there [ref:wiki-kangaroo].

## 2. Stalking alone

**Palmer River, Musgrave and the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay** (Roth's closest record to Western Yalanji country and to the Hann River) [ref:roth1901]:

1. Find fresh sign on a pad or a grazing flat (see *Signs*).
2. **Track the animal from downwind.** Keep the wind in your face the whole approach.
3. Use the ground. Roth's hunter did not want to 'run the risk of exposing his presence' [ref:roth1901]; the dictionary's words for it are **[karangaji](word:karangaji)** 'stalk', **[karangal](word:karangal)** 'sneak around to see, reconnoiter', **[durrubu dungay](word:durrubu dungay)** 'walk on tiptoe' and **[mingki-janay](word:mingki-janay)** 'squat, crouch' [ref:hershberger1982].
4. When the animal is feeding with its head down, move; when it stands up and looks, freeze. A grazer's day is 'rest ... in the shade' and 'graze ... in the late afternoon' [ref:nesp-agile], and a resting animal in shade is the one Roth's North-West hunters crept up on in the heat [ref:roth1897].
5. Get to spear range, which with a [woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera) is a matter of tens of metres, and throw at the body. The dictionary's **[mungkil](word:mungkil)** is 'spear to kill' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Pennefather River, the camouflage stalk** (west Cape York, labelled as such) [ref:roth1901]: 'If by himself the hunter will paint himself completely over with yellow ochre (with this pigment or earth rubbed well into his arm-pits, etc., so as to kill the smell of his perspiration), and make himself resemble an ant-bed under the guise of which he can gradually approach to within a very short distance.' Two tricks in one: the [ochre](entry:red-ochre) hides the hunter's smell at its source, and his shape becomes a [termite mound](entry:termites-and-ant-beds), which a kangaroo sees every day and ignores.

**Bloomfield River** [ref:anderson1996]: 'Other kangaroos and wallabies were stalked from down wind at times and places where they were known to graze, rest or come for water.' Bennett's tree-kangaroo 'was tracked by sight or with the use of dogs' [ref:anderson1996].

## 3. The scent trick: moving the animal with a spare spear

This is Roth's record from the Palmer, the Musgrave and Princess Charlotte Bay, and it is the one piece of the old method that uses the animal's nose against it [ref:roth1901]:

1. The hunter is downwind of a kangaroo that is 'in some brush-wood' or too far off for a sure throw.
2. He takes a spare spear and smears it 'with the perspiration from under the arm-pits or crutch', so that it is 'fully charged with the concentrated essence of humanity'.
3. He throws it 'well over its head into the ground beyond', so that it lands **upwind** of the animal.
4. 'The wind carries the scent and drives the kangaroo from apparent into real danger': the animal moves away from the smell, towards the hidden hunter, and into range.
5. '(Wallabies are similarly hunted in these same districts.)'

Nothing in the record uses smoke this way. The hunters masked their own scent with ochre, kept it behind them with the wind, and used a dose of it to push the animal. Fire, when it was used, was used to drive, and on a different scale (see 5).

## 4. Two hunters: the drive to a waiting spearman

The smallest drive in the record is two people, and it is the Bloomfield's normal hunting party: 'at most two men going out for one to two days' [ref:anderson1996]. The Pennefather version is the pattern: 'a general drive may be organised, the younger men hunting the animals into the direction of the older ones who are in waiting with their spears' [ref:roth1901]. Putting the record and the animals' habits together:

1. **Agree the ground first.** The waiting spearman takes a fixed, known position on the animals' retreat line: a pad to water, a gap in the timber, a saddle between ridges, the place the mob always crosses. In every recorded drive the waiting men stood at known points, the 'openings' of the Bloomfield fire wall or the ends of the Pennefather arc [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901], so that the beaters knew exactly where the spears were.
2. **The spearman goes in downwind** of where the animals are feeding, and settles where he can see the line without showing on the skyline. He waits: **[kujil](word:kujil)** 'keep, hold, wait for' [ref:hershberger1982].
3. **The driver comes in from the far side, upwind if possible**, so that the animals catch his scent and move away from it, slowly, towards the spearman. A slow push is what you want; Roth's drives used shouting to make the kangaroo run 'headlong' into a net [ref:roth1901], but a spear needs an animal that stops.
4. **Read the mob, not the animal.** The grey rests in groups 'around the middle of the day' and splits into small feeding groups [ref:wiki-eastern-grey]; the whiptail mob has guards [ref:wiki-whiptail]; the antilopine mob bunches 'as a response to threats from humans or dingoes' [ref:wiki-antilopine]. The first animal to stand tall and face you is the sentry, and the mob moves when it does.
5. **Keep the river in mind.** It is not a wall. 'Kangaroos and wallabies are adept swimmers, and often flee into waterways if presented with the option' [ref:wiki-kangaroo]; the Tully people used that, driving wallabies into floodwater and killing them there [ref:roth1901]. In the dry, a river of pools and dry sand is a path as much as a barrier.
6. **Signal without sound.** Roth's districts had hand signs for the animals and the hunt [ref:roth1908]; the dictionary has **[kawal](word:kawal)** 'a shout, cooee, not far away', **[ngawungkal](word:ngawungkal)** 'a shout from a long ways away' and **[kuwimbur](word:kuwimbur)** 'whistle' for when quiet no longer matters [ref:hershberger1982].

## 5. Many hunters: circles, fires and beaters

**The circle (Pennefather River)** [ref:roth1901]: 'If a hunting-party can be formed, the individuals composing it will spread out and gradually circle round the locality in which the kangaroos have been observed to be sheltering, and so gradually diminish the contained area.'

**The three-quarter circle of fire (Pennefather River)** [ref:roth1901]: 'in the circling method just mentioned, instead of closing in on the marsupials in the centre, a three-quarter circle of fires may be lighted, the best spear-throwers watching for the animals to emerge from between its two extremities.'

**The line of fire (Cape Bedford, Guugu Yimithirr country)** [ref:roth1901]: 'the whole camp will go and start a long line of bush-fires, up to a mile long, extending to the summit of some hill if possible: the men will then form in line at intervals, and so circle round, spearing the kangaroos in between them and the row of fires.'

**The wall of fire (Bloomfield River, Kuku Yalanji)** [ref:anderson1996]: 'Fires were carefully lit to create a "wall" of fire going in one direction with only a few openings. Young people, starting within a forested area, walked in a long line beating the bush and shouting. This drove kangaroos, wallabies and other smaller animals towards the gaps in the fire, where the older men waited with spears.' The [hunting with fire](entry:hunting-with-fire) page has this in full, with the law on it.

**Beaters into nets and cages (Atherton)** [ref:roth1901]: for the kangaroo, 'the kangaroo, driven headlong by the shouts of the hunters, lying more or less in ambush, finds itself suddenly entangled in the meshes, tumbles over in its attempts at extrication, and is soon despatched with spears and sticks'. For the wallaby, 'all the women and children will "beat" a considerable area of scrub country, and, what with shouting and hooting, easily drive the wallabies into and along their accustomed tracks, and so into the cages which are there fixed in position'.

**Beaters into a net enclosure (Boulia district, North-West)** [ref:roth1897] [ref:roth1901]: 'they may be driven into an enclosure formed of three nets fixed in the position somewhat of the three sides of a square: the hunters, having previously determined upon the locality where the kangaroos are encamped, will drive them into this enclosure with the assistance of numerous "beaters" stationed in such manner as to compel the animals running into the required direction' (Roth's 1897 Plate XI, fig. 232, shown on this page).

All of these are whole-camp, dry-season work, lit and placed with care, with the spearmen standing at agreed points. None of them is a small fire lit on the morning.

## 6. The gear: nets, cages and pits

**The Atherton kangaroo net** (Roth's Figs. 20–21, on this page) [ref:roth1901]. Made 'from what the Ngatchan [people] call the *kewan*, *Sterculia quadrifida*', the [kurrajong](entry:kurrajong), whose fibre-twine was 'used for the large kangaroo-nets at Atherton' [ref:roth1901-string]. 'The net is woven on a mesh similar to that of a fishing-net ... the particular specimen in my possession having occupied the whole local camp some three weeks in completing. The fibre-twine employed is well over ¼-inch in diameter, and of the ordinary double-ply: each mesh can be stretched to over a foot in length. The body of the net runs on a top- and bottom- string ... attached by slip-knots to two strong side-supports between 3½ feet and 4 feet long, firmly implanted in the ground at a distance of some 16 feet or 18 feet apart ... Three or four intermediate supports ... on front and back, keep the net itself upright; they are made of comparatively light switches, and vary in length so as to stretch the net to a greater extent at the centre than at the sides. The top-string rests on the fork of the most central of these supports ... None of these intermediate supports are fixed into the ground, the weight of the net being sufficient to keep them in position.' 'When not in use, the net is rolled round the two side-supports and carried by a stout cord, looped at either extremity; this cord is held either in the hand or, far more commonly, slung over the shoulder' [ref:roth1901]. See [nets](entry:nets) and [string and twine](entry:string-and-twine).

**The Atherton wallaby cage, *yingkar*** (Roth's Figs. 22–23, on this page) [ref:roth1901]: 'a cylindrical basket from 4 to 4½ feet long, and up to about 1 foot in diameter, with a pointed extremity and enlarged half-funnel shaped mouth', made of split [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) [ref:roth1901-string]. 'Several such traps, from ten to twelve of them, are put into use on the one expedition by laying them lengthways along the wallaby tracks which have been previously and carefully noted. Each is so placed as to have its funnel or hood up, the open extremity being surrounded with bushes and pieces of bark. The trap proves itself efficacious, owing to the circumstance, pointed out to me by [the hunters], that when a wallaby is hard pressed and makes for shelter it runs with the head down: instead of attempting to jump over, and its attempts are frustrated by the artificial bush work, the animal accordingly forces itself into the trap, the slope of the hood still further guiding its direction, where, tightly jambed, it is soon despatched by a hunter watching in close proximity.'

**Pits (Cape Grafton, Cairns and Atherton)** [ref:roth1901]: 'intended primarily for breaking the animal's leg', the pits 'are covered with cross-sticks, upon which sheaves of grass, soil, etc., are laid so as to make the supposititious level appear flush with and of the same nature as the surrounding surface. The cross-sticks may be tied and fixed in position with twine, as well as supported by uprights from below; the pits I have observed from 6 to 8 feet wide, but not more than 2½ feet deep.'

**Nets elsewhere.** Wallabies 'used to be caught with nets on the Herbert River (according to Lumholtz, the nets were from 15 to 20 feet long, with large mesh), on the lower Tully River, etc.', and Leichhardt saw kangaroo nets 'of *Sterculia* fibre' on the Dawson [ref:roth1901]. In the Boulia district the emu-net rig of forked uprights and a top string (Roth's fig. 226) doubled as a kangaroo net, 'quickly rigged up along their beaten tracks to water' [ref:roth1897]. There is no record of a kangaroo net on the Bloomfield or the Palmer; the Bloomfield traded nets in from the Laura [ref:roth1910b14].

## 7. Dogs and water

**North-West Central districts** [ref:roth1897] [ref:roth1901]: 'in rainy weather, and over boggy soil, they are run down with dogs.' **Palmer and Princess Charlotte Bay**: 'in addition to occasionally hunting them with dogs, kangaroos are speared' [ref:roth1901]. **Lower Tully**: wallabies hunted 'occasionally with dogs' and, in flood, driven 'from off the higher levels into the water' [ref:roth1901]. **Bloomfield**: boys 'had dingo pups as pets while they were being trained for hunting' [ref:anderson1996], and the tree-kangaroo 'was tracked by sight or with the use of dogs' [ref:anderson1996]. The [dingo and dogs](entry:dingo-and-dogs) page has the training.

## 8. The kill, the carcass and the cook

**Tendons first.** On the Pennefather a kangaroo 'on being killed, is usually first of all robbed of its tail-tendons' [ref:roth1901]: cut round the tail at the butt, break the tail back and the long tendons draw out of the sheath. They dry into *[biyal](word:biyal)* [ref:hershberger1982]; the [sinew](entry:sinew) page has the rest.

**The Bloomfield way: break the bones and put it on the fire** [ref:anderson1996]: 'Many meat items, including reptiles, birds, wallabies and other marsupials were cooked straight on the fire after their bodies had been bashed with an axe to break the bones.' The dictionary's **[dindal](word:dindal)** is 'to roast on coals', **[wayjul](word:wayjul)** 'to cook food; to burn something', **[balnji](word:balnji)** 'doing something right; properly with a fire as in cooking', **[jani](word:jani)** 'well cooked, done' and **[kidal](word:kidal)** 'clean an animal, to remove the insides' [ref:hershberger1982]. Nuts that were not 'eaten on their own, were added to wallaby carcasses to add flavour during cooking' [ref:anderson1996].

**The Bloomfield and Cape Bedford earth oven** (*[kurrma](word:kurrma)*) [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982]:

1. Heat 'a number of stones' well in a fire, then remove them 'together with the ashes'.
2. Quickly dig 'a hole ... in the position just occupied'.
3. Line the bottom with 'several kinds of leaves (various species of ginger)', the [wild ginger](entry:wild-ginger) of the scrub.
4. Lay in 'the pieces of meat, amongst which the hot stones and ashes are packed'.
5. Cover with 'some more leaves or tea-tree bark, and lastly a layer of earth and stones'.

The stones were handled with **[bangkal](word:bangkal)**, 'tongs made from voya vine, used in cooking in a kurrma', and the oven could be covered with **[dukul-dukul](word:dukul-dukul)**, the 'broad-leafed bush that can be used as cover for a dirt oven' [ref:hershberger1982]. The [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) page has the whole method.

**The Pennefather whole-roast** (west Cape York) [ref:roth1901]: after the tail-tendons, the kangaroo 'has the main joints of its upper and lower limbs dislocated to enable them to be subsequently folded over and bound together. The tongue is next drawn out and skewered with a wooden splinter over the incisors (required for spoke-shaves) to prevent them being too much damaged by the heat. The belly, incised horizontally, is now freed of its intestines, which are replaced by heated stones. The limbs are finally drawn up to the sides of the body, the whole covered with bark, tied round and round like a bundle, and put into the hot ashes, etc., with which it is well covered over.'

**Carrying home.** A small wallaby went in the men's stretching *Ficus*-twine bag [ref:anderson1996]; the net went home 'rolled round the two side-supports' and slung over the shoulder [ref:roth1901].

## 9. What the record does not say

The record does not say how each people hunted on its own country, what they called the drive, which animals they preferred, or how the meat was shared. It does not describe hunting with firearms, which is what Anderson found in the 1970s: 'for land hunting .22 rifles were almost exclusively used' [ref:anderson1996], and the dictionary's *[mirrba](word:mirrba)*, the woomera, had come to mean 'also rifle' [ref:hershberger1982]. All of that is for the contribution box.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**The animal.** 'Whilst many people see large male kangaroos as placid grazing animals. The reality is that they can be aggressive towards people. Although the risk of this happening is very small, we still need to be wary around them.' 'Females with joeys that are old enough to be out of the pouch can also become aggressive if they feel that the presence of a person is a possible threat to their young.' 'Both male and female kangaroos are large, powerful, wild animals that are capable of inflicting injury on people' [ref:qld-kangaroos]. If one comes at you: 'move away as slowly as possible to a safe place. Give a short, deep cough; avoid eye contact; bow your head; and keep your arms close to your body as you move away ... Do not turn your back on the animal or run. Where possible put a barrier between you and the animal such as a tree or fence' [ref:qld-kangaroos]. A wounded animal in the water is the most dangerous of all: a large kangaroo 'may use its forepaws to hold the predator underwater so as to drown it' [ref:wiki-kangaroo].

**Rivers.** Before you wade any river, read the [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles) page and the notes for your place below.

**Two hunters, one line of fire.** In every recorded drive the spearmen stood at agreed, fixed points and the beaters knew them [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901]. Split up only after you have both agreed where each of you will be, where the animals are expected to go, and that no spear or shot goes toward the other's ground. Settle the signals before you part: **[kawal](word:kawal)** 'a shout, cooee, not far away', **[ngawungkal](word:ngawungkal)** 'a shout from a long ways away', **[kuwimbur](word:kuwimbur)** 'whistle' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Heat.** Carry water; the animals are in the shade for a reason.

**Fire.** A grass fire in October woodland 'can be severe and widespread' [ref:pbg-cape-york]. A fire larger than 2 m in any direction needs a permit from the local Fire Warden, no fire may be lit during a fire ban, and the occupier is responsible for any fire on the land [ref:qfd] [ref:qfes-pp]. On the hunting side, nothing in the record uses smoke to hide a hunter's scent: the scent methods were the wind, the ochre and the scent-charged spear [ref:roth1901], and the fires were drives, lit by whole camps in a planned line [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]. A small fire lit upwind of a mob on the morning sends them the hunter's smoke and the hunter's scent together, and Cook's note that kangaroos were 'so much afraid of fire' [ref:roth1901] says which way they will go.

**The meat.** Follow the old rule: a lean animal in poor condition, *[jirrburr](word:jirrburr)*, 'will not be eaten' [ref:hershberger1982]. Lean meat dries and toughens fast [ref:wiki-kangaroo-meat]; cook it through, **[jani](word:jani)** 'well cooked, done' [ref:hershberger1982]. Carcasses for the commercial trade are 'bled and eviscerated in the field' and kept cold [ref:wiki-kangaroo-meat], and the bush rule is the same: clean the animal at once, keep it in shade and get it cooked or cold.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Protected animals.** 'Kangaroos are protected native wildlife under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*' and 'it is an offence to harm or kill kangaroos without a damage mitigation permit' [ref:qld-kangaroos] [ref:qld-nca]. The commercial harvest is separate: 'kangaroos are harvested by licensed shooters in accordance with a strict code of practice', in 'designated harvest zones' that close 'if numbers approach minimum thresholds' [ref:wiki-kangaroo-meat].

**Native title.** Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* protects native title holders who hunt 'for the purpose of satisfying their personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs' from the licence and permit rules that bind everyone else [ref:alrc-s211]. The determinations that set out those rights differ from place to place: see each place below. The [law on hunting](entry:law-hunting-and-fishing) page sets out the layers.

**The small ones.** The northern bettong is 'endangered', with 'only two known populations in the Mareeba region' and 'an estimated ... 1000 left in the wild'; 'a Recovery Team including government agencies, scientists, traditional owners and volunteer groups' is working on its habitat [ref:wiki-northern-bettong]. The Mareeba rock-wallaby is 'near-threatened' [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby].

**Time and country:** *[mudu wayjul](word:mudu wayjul)* 'the time just before daylight, pre-dawn'; *[muduwaju](word:muduwaju)* 'dawn, daybreak, early morning'; *[wunkuwingku](word:wunkuwingku)* 'morning'; *[yilay-yilay](word:yilay-yilay)* 'late afternoon, when the sun is in the west'; *[wujurr](word:wujurr)* 'darkness, night'; *[kunarangkal](word:kunarangkal)* 'middle of the night'; *[wabarr](word:wabarr)* 'shade'; *[jikan](word:jikan)* 'grass'; *[duli](word:duli)* 'burnt patch of grass'; *[ngalku](word:ngalku)* 'bush fire'; *[madja](word:madja)* 'scrub, jungle, rain forest'; *[kima-kima](word:kima-kima)* 'easy crossing of water' [ref:hershberger1982].
