locations.summary: On the Hann the kangaroo family means above all the **agile wallaby**: downstream in Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park 'agile wallabies are abundant and can often be seen grazing or sleeping' in the open woodlands and grasslands [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. This is not Kuku Yalanji country. The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, and people of both told the Federal Court they hunt wallabies and kangaroos on it [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Kuku Thaypan Elders burn the boxwood country to bring the wallabies onto new grass, and used fire to steer them to the hunters [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Names here
Which ones live here
sections.body:
The Atlas of Living Australia holds 141 records of the kangaroo family from 1975 to 2026 in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru: **agile wallaby 99**, eastern grey kangaroo 18, spectacled hare-wallaby 13, common wallaroo 4, antilopine kangaroo 3, northern nailtail wallaby 3 and Cape York rock-wallaby 1, with a single rufous bettong (2014) [ref:ala-hann]. In the park 'the less common northern nailtail wallaby is more elusive', and the spectacled hare-wallaby is one of its threatened species [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture].

They graze the open country along the river: stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark 'with a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann], and the Molloy box (*Ku ronga*) woodland of the Hann's floodplains [ref:standley2019]. The Kuku Thaypan Elders count the boxwood country among the 'important hunting and hence feeding areas for large marsupials, areas burnt traditionally to attract game' [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Their year here
sections.body:
In the wet, December to March, the rivers flood onto the plains, and 'during this time animals disperse far and wide as food and water is plentiful'. From April the floodplains dry out, 'and by October the land is brown and parched' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Hann itself has not stopped running on any day since its gauge was put in in 1968, though by September–November it is very low [ref:bom-105001b].

The Elders' early-dry burns make the feed. 'Removal of old grass enables perennial grasses to produce new growth, high in nutrients for wallabies', and the thesis shows a female agile wallaby, *nyeh myra*, 'enjoying grass regrowth resulting from an early season burn' [ref:standley2019]. For one of their lagoons, the Elders listed an 'increase in number of Agile wallaby' among the signs that the country was coming back to health [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: How people hunted them here
sections.body:
**With fire (Kuku Thaypan Elders).** 'Fire was also used to direct animals such as wallabies to areas where it was easier to hunt them. The old people knew where the animals travelled every day, could track them and use fire to contain them on areas where they could more easily be caught or speared' [ref:standley2019]. Standley's field records put the method in one line: 'The careful use of fire is like "watering the garden"' [ref:standley2019].

**Stalking (Palmer, Musgrave and Princess Charlotte Bay, about 1900).** Roth's record from the districts around the Hann is the one in *The hunt* above: kangaroos tracked 'from the windward', the spare spear charged with the hunter's sweat and thrown beyond the animal to push it onto him, wallabies 'similarly hunted in these same districts', and dogs used occasionally [ref:roth1901]. At Princess Charlotte Bay there were hand signs for the male and female kangaroo and the brown kangaroo, so the hunt could go on in silence [ref:roth1908].

**Today.** A Thaypan man told the Court: 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels' [ref:fca-thaypan]. A Possum man spoke of 'hunting pigs, kangaroos, goanna, porcupine, and plain turkeys' [ref:fca-possum].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
The Federal Court recognised native title over the Hann on 2 November 2023: the **upper Hann** is the Possum People's country, held by the Possum Aboriginal Corporation [ref:fca-possum]; the **middle and lower Hann** are Thaypan country, held by the Awu-Laya Indigenous Corporation [ref:fca-thaypan]. Downstream, Rinyirru's Traditional Owners are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples, and the park is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Native title holders may hunt for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs without the licences others need [ref:nta1993]; everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission to be on their country.

Standley records kangaroo and wallaby story places and boundary markers on Thaypan country [ref:standley2019]. Those stories belong to their custodians: ask them, not this page.

locations.summary: Around [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the Atlas of Living Australia records eight members of the family: the agile wallaby, the common wallaroo, the eastern grey kangaroo, the whiptail wallaby, the antilopine kangaroo, two rock-wallabies and, rarely, the red-legged pademelon, with two bettongs beside them [ref:ala-macropods]. The Western Yalanji words and ways are for the contribution box.

sections.heading: Names here
sections.body: We found no Western Yalanji wallaby or kangaroo words in the published dictionary, which was compiled on the coast; the names used on the Mitchell for the wallaroo of the ridges, the rock-wallaby of the range tops and the whiptail of the hills are the first thing to ask for.

sections.heading: The animals of the Mitchell
Signs here
sections.body: In the dry season on the Mitchell the water is the chain of [waterholes](entry:waterhole), and the pads run down to them from the ridges through the [woodland](entry:woodland).

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body:
Kangaroo grass and black speargrass are among the most-recorded plants within 30 km of the Karma Waters homestead, under the ironbark, box and bloodwood of the [woodland](entry:woodland) [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:re-woodland]. On a station of 'rolling hills' the rock piles, the gorges and the stony ridge tops are a different country from the flats, with a different wallaby on them.

**Western Yalanji country, close in.** Within 30 km of the Karma Waters homestead the Atlas holds only six records of the whole family: three wallaroos, one agile wallaby, one antilopine kangaroo and one Mareeba rock-wallaby. Within 60 km it holds 417, and 149 of them were made in 2024 alone [ref:ala-macropods]. That is a statement about how few people have recorded wildlife on the upper Mitchell, not about how few animals there are. The country 'in and around the Palmer and Mitchell River systems which lie to the north-west of Mt Carbine' is the Western Yalanji determination country [ref:brady2013], and a wallaby count by the people who live on it would be worth more than the Atlas.

**Where to look at Karma Waters.** The grazers come onto the river flats and the grassy flats between the ridges in the late afternoon and the early morning and rest in shade through the day [ref:nesp-agile] [ref:wiki-eastern-grey] [ref:qld-kangaroos]. The wallaroo is on the stony hills and moves at night [ref:wiki-wallaroo]. The rock-wallabies are on the range tops and the gorges [ref:wiki-rock-wallaby]. Nobody has recorded a bettong closer than the 60 km circle [ref:ala-macropods]; whether the *[jayju](word:jayju)* is still digging on the Mitchell is a question for the contribution box.

sections.heading: Fire here
sections.body: The Queensland Herbarium's guideline for the Mitchell woodland asks for 'low, with occasional moderate' burns at two-to-five-year intervals, less than 40% of the landscape in any year, with long-unburnt patches kept 'to maintain a diversity of habitat for wildlife' [ref:re-woodland]. Down the river at Kowanyama, Traditional Owner Clarita Yam put it in one sentence: 'when you burn too much, you burn out your Country and there's nothing left for your cattle, wallabies and kangaroo' [ref:kowanyama2024].

sections.heading: Seasons here
sections.body:
The bad fire-weather days at Palmerville, the nearest long record to Karma Waters, average about 36 °C with about 18% humidity [ref:pbg-cape-york]. Carry water.

**What the Atlas says about months.** Records of the family within 60 km of Karma Waters peak in November (116) and October (52), with April (48) and May (41) next and almost nothing in February and March [ref:ala-macropods]. That is the calendar of visitors with cameras, who come in the dry and leave before the wet, rather than the calendar of the animals, and it says nothing about when they are easiest to find.

sections.heading: Hunting here
sections.body: The published record does not say how Western Yalanji people hunted on the Mitchell, what they called the drive, which animals they preferred, or how the meat was shared. The nearest record is Roth's from the Palmer, in *The hunt* above [ref:roth1901]. At Karma Waters today, hunting dogs are not allowed on the station [ref:kw-induction].

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body:
**The river.** Crossing the Mitchell means crossing crocodile country; read the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) and [saltwater crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile) pages before you wade, and cross where the dictionary's **[kima-kima](word:kima-kima)** applies, 'easy crossing of water, water isn't rushing' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Fire.** The 2013 and 2026 Western Yalanji determinations expressly exclude lighting fires 'for the purpose of hunting' [ref:brady2013] [ref:fca2026wy].

**Firearms on a pastoral lease.** Under the 2013 determination, hunting with firearms on a pastoral lease may happen only where stock are not present and after the lessee has had enough notice to deal with safety [ref:brady2013]. At Karma Waters the station's induction does not allow weapons or hunting dogs [ref:kw-induction].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
**Native title.** The 2013 Western Yalanji determinations over country 'in and around the Palmer and Mitchell River systems which lie to the north-west of Mt Carbine' recognise non-exclusive rights to 'hunt, fish and gather on the land and waters of the area for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal purposes', and their fire right is to 'light fires ... for domestic purposes including cooking, but not for the purpose of hunting or clearing vegetation'; hunting with firearms on a pastoral lease is allowed only where stock are not present and after notice to the lessee [ref:brady2013]. The 2026 determination that finished the Cape York claims for the Western Yalanji allows fires 'for cultural, spiritual or domestic purposes including cooking, but not for the purpose of hunting or clearing vegetation' [ref:fca2026wy].

**Karma Waters.** The station falls under the 1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen* consent determination, the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia [ref:kw-about] [ref:wyac2020]. Its published summary recognises rights to use the area and its natural resources for 'social, cultural, economic, religious, spiritual, customary and traditional purposes' and says nothing about fire either way [ref:wyac2020]. The station burns 'most of our country' on a three-to-four-year cycle, depending on the seasons, to clear fuel and control weeds [ref:kw-land]; visitors' campfires are restricted to the campsite, and weapons and hunting dogs are not allowed [ref:kw-induction]. Permission to hunt on this country comes from the Traditional Owners and the station together, and the [Karma Waters guide](place:karma-waters) says how to ask.

**Fire coming back.** The Western Yalanji say their country has 'suffered from wildfires since traditional burning practices all but ceased in the 20th century', and have begun a savanna burning project [ref:wyac2020].

**The small ones.** The northern bettong and the Mareeba rock-wallaby are both of concern (see *On Country today* above). A record of either from the upper Mitchell would matter.

**For the contribution box.** The Western Yalanji words for the wallaroo, the rock-wallaby, the whiptail, the grey, the joey and the bettong; which of the dictionary's nine words is which animal; how the two-person drive was and is done on the Mitchell, who waits and who walks; whether hand signs were used; which animals were preferred and in which months; how the meat was shared; what was done with the skin; and any family memory of the old fire drives and the old nets on this side of the range.

locations.summary: Kangaroos and wallabies were 'the major meat-resource animals which were hunted' on the Bloomfield [ref:anderson1996]. Up in the rainforest trees of the coast live the tree-kangaroos, **[murral](word:murral)** [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Names here
sections.body: **Place names.** The dictionary records *[Mijinan](word:Mijinan)* as 'where the bridge is over Wallabay Creek (place name)', on Eastern Kuku Yalanji country [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Rainforest
sections.body: On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country the rainforest has its own members of the family. Bennett's tree-kangaroo lives 'almost completely on the leaves of a wide range of rainforest trees' in the forests between Cooktown and the Daintree, and 'is also occasionally found in sclerophyll woodlands' [ref:wiki-bennett]; the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service records *murral* among the tree-dwelling animals the Eastern Kuku Yalanji hunted [ref:qpws-daintree].

sections.heading: The Bloomfield year
sections.body:
**The dry: branch camps and drives.** Anderson's reconstruction of the Bloomfield year has the small family groups moving out in the dry 'away from the main camping areas' to 'set up temporary "branch" camps in order to exploit non-seasonal opportunistic resources such as eelfish, tortoises, wallabies and goannas', while the coastal people made 'seasonal forays inland up onto the coastal ranges for wallaby, yams and tubers' [ref:anderson1996]. The big [fire drives](entry:hunting-with-fire) were a dry-season thing: 'Kuku-Yalanji hunting on land was essentially a solitary affair, with at most two men going out for one to two days. The exception was the large-scale wallaby drives undertaken in the dry season' [ref:anderson1996].

**The wet.** 'In the wet, the tendency was to contract into larger more permanent camps' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
**Native title.** The 2007 Eastern Kuku Yalanji determination recognises the right to hunt animals, not for trade or commerce [ref:walker2007].

**Hunting as it is done.** By the time Anderson did his fieldwork on the Bloomfield in the 1970s, 'for land hunting .22 rifles were almost exclusively used', while 'the stone ovens were often used for cooking meat in the bush camps I stayed in' [ref:anderson1996]. The dictionary records the same shift in one word: *[mirrba](word:mirrba)* is the woomera, 'also rifle' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Fire coming back.** On the coast the Eastern Kuku Yalanji are rekindling a cultural-burning regime [ref:newsport]. The Daintree, Ngalba Bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks were handed back to the Eastern Kuku Yalanji in 2021 and are jointly managed with the state until Traditional Owners take over [ref:handback2021]. Bennett's tree-kangaroo, 'now that it is rarely hunted by Aboriginal Australians', has 'numbers ... increasing and its range expanding', 'likely because most of its range is now protected under World Heritage legislation' [ref:wiki-bennett].
